channel.title: Triggers on Best of AI
channel.description: Recent content in Triggers on Best of AI

item.title: Bardeen
item.description:
Bardeen automates repetitive work that happens on web pages. A user installs the extension, then runs playbooks that click through sites, extract data, and send it elsewhere. Typical uses include scraping lists of people from LinkedIn into Google Sheets, saving a company’s details to a CRM, or sending a meeting summary to Slack.

A natural language builder lets users describe what they want, and the AI assembles the steps, which can be edited. Triggers run automations on a schedule or when something happens, and integrations cover hundreds of apps. Sales and recruiting teams, who spend time moving data between tabs, are heavy users.

item.title: Boomi
item.description:
Boomi was one of the first cloud integration platforms. Its visual builder lets teams connect applications and move data between them, with a large catalog of connectors, API management, data integration, and workflow automation in one platform. Companies use it to sync records between sales, finance, HR, and operations systems without extensive custom code.

The company has leaned into AI agents. Boomi lets teams build agents that use connected systems as tools, and offers an agent catalog and controls to track what agents are allowed to do, which matters as companies deploy many of them. Data management and master data tools help keep records consistent across systems.

item.title: SAP Signavio
item.description:
Signavio helps companies understand how their processes really work. Teams model processes in a visual notation so everyone can see the intended steps, owners, and rules, and store them in a shared repository. This makes it easier to document, improve, and standardize work across departments.

Process mining adds evidence. By reading event logs from systems like SAP ERP, it reconstructs what happened in practice, revealing delays, rework, and variants that differ from the designed flow. Analysts can then quantify the impact and decide what to fix. Collaboration and journey modeling tools help teams plan transformations such as moving to a new ERP.

item.title: Celonis
item.description:
Celonis is the best-known process mining platform. Every action in business systems, such as creating an order or approving an invoice, leaves a record with a time stamp. Celonis reads these logs and rebuilds the real process, showing the paths that cases take, where they wait, and how often they deviate from the intended flow.

With that picture, teams find delays, rework, and costly exceptions. The platform quantifies the impact, suggests improvements, and can trigger automated actions or alerts. AI features answer questions about process data and recommend where to focus. Common uses include order-to-cash, procure-to-pay, and supply chain work.

item.title: JITX
item.description:
JITX approaches board design as software. Instead of drawing a schematic by hand, an engineer describes circuits and requirements in code, and the system selects parts, creates connections, and generates a board layout that satisfies rules for signal integrity, power, and manufacturing. Changes can be made by editing the description and regenerating.

That makes it easier to reuse designs, check them automatically, and explore alternatives. The platform’s solvers handle routine layout tasks, so engineers concentrate on architecture. It targets hardware teams that build complex boards and want faster iteration.

item.title: Make
item.description: Make, formerly called Integromat, lets you automate work between apps by drawing it. You place modules on a canvas for each app, such as Gmail, Google Sheets, Slack, or a CRM, and connect them with lines that show how data flows. You can add routers that split the flow into branches, filters that decide which items continue, iterators that handle lists, and functions that change data on the way. This visual layout makes complicated logic easier to follow than a long linear list of steps.

item.title: Microsoft Power Automate
item.description:
Power Automate connects apps and automates repetitive work. Users build flows that trigger on events, such as an email arriving or a form submission, and perform actions in hundreds of services. It works smoothly with Teams, SharePoint, Outlook, and Dynamics.

AI features extend it. Copilot lets people describe a flow in plain language, AI Builder processes documents and forms, and agent capabilities handle more open-ended tasks. Desktop flows use robotic process automation to control applications that have no API.

item.title: Microsoft Power Automate
item.description:
Power Automate helps people automate repetitive work without code. In a visual designer, users create flows that start from a trigger, such as an email arriving or a form being submitted, and then run actions like saving attachments, updating a spreadsheet, sending approvals, or posting to Teams. It connects to hundreds of services, with deep integration with SharePoint, Outlook, Excel, and Dynamics 365, and handles scheduled and event-driven tasks.

It also covers robotic process automation. Desktop flows record and replay actions on a computer, allowing automation of legacy applications that lack APIs. AI Builder adds capabilities such as reading text from documents, classifying content, and making predictions, and Copilot can build a flow from a plain-language description. Newer features support AI agents that use flows as tools.

item.title: n8n
item.description: n8n lets you build automations by connecting nodes on a canvas, similar to Zapier or Make, but with more room for code. Each node is a step: a trigger like a webhook or schedule, an action in an app, or a block that transforms data with JavaScript or Python. Hundreds of integrations are included, and a generic HTTP node covers the rest. Workflows can branch, loop, and call other workflows, so it handles anything from simple notifications to elaborate data pipelines.

item.title: Nintex
item.description:
Nintex helps organizations digitize their processes. Using a visual designer, business analysts build workflows that route requests, collect approvals, update systems, and send notifications, and they create forms to start those workflows. It integrates with Microsoft 365, SharePoint, Salesforce, and many other systems, which is where its roots lie, with many customers automating processes on SharePoint.

The platform has several parts. Process mapping tools document how work actually happens, automation tools execute workflows and robotic process automation, and document generation tools produce contracts and reports from data. AI features assist with building workflows from descriptions and extracting data from documents, and analytics show where processes slow down.

item.title: Tray.io
item.description:
Tray.io builds on the idea of integration-platform-as-a-service. Teams use a visual builder to create workflows that connect SaaS applications, databases, and internal systems, with powerful logic, error handling, and the ability to write code where necessary. Hundreds of connectors and a universal connector for APIs cover common enterprise tools such as Salesforce, Workday, and Slack.

The company has moved toward AI agents. Its Merlin AI tools let teams build agents that use the connected systems as tools, so an agent can look up a customer, update a record, and send a message, with governance over what it can access. Embedded integration products let software companies offer customer-facing integrations in their own products.

item.title: UiPath
item.description:
UiPath popularized robotic process automation, in which software robots mimic what a person does on a screen. Developers build automations in a studio by recording and arranging steps such as clicking, copying data between systems, and filling forms, and run them on servers or desktops. This is valuable for companies with legacy systems that lack APIs, since bots can work through the same interfaces people use.

The platform has expanded into AI. Document understanding extracts data from invoices and forms, process mining reveals which workflows are worth automating, and agent tools let AI agents plan and carry out tasks, orchestrated alongside robots and people. The Maestro orchestration layer coordinates agents, robots, and human steps, and governance features control access and auditing.

item.title: Workato
item.description:
Workato is an integration and automation platform. Teams build recipes that link applications such as Salesforce, Workday, and Slack, trigger actions, and move data. Business users can create simple automations while IT governs the platform.

The company has added AI across the product. Users describe a workflow in plain language and Workato builds a draft, document understanding extracts data, and agents handle tasks with enterprise controls. Governance, security, and monitoring suit regulated companies.

item.title: Zapier
item.description:
Zapier handles the plumbing between business apps. A workflow listens for an event in one tool and does something in another, with filters, paths, and delays to model real processes. Templates cover common needs in sales, marketing, and operations.

Newer capabilities include AI actions that read and write text, agents that carry out multi-step tasks, and an MCP offering that exposes Zapier actions to AI assistants. Teams can monitor runs, handle errors, and manage access centrally.

item.title: Zapier
item.description: Zapier connects the apps a business already uses and lets them pass data to each other without code. You build a Zap with a trigger, such as a new form submission, and one or more actions, such as adding a row to a spreadsheet, posting in Slack, and creating a CRM contact. It supports thousands of apps, from Gmail and Salesforce to niche tools, which is the main reason people choose it over building integrations by hand. Filters, paths, and delays let a Zap branch and wait, and a multi-step workflow can handle surprisingly complicated processes.

item.title: Relay
item.description:
Relay.app takes the Zapier-style approach and adds two things: AI steps and humans in the loop. A workflow can trigger on an event, call an AI to summarize or draft, then pause for a teammate to approve before the next action runs. This suits tasks where full automation is risky.

Integrations connect common business tools, and a visual builder makes flows easy to design. Examples include drafting replies for review, routing leads, and preparing reports. Approvals can be done in email or Slack.

item.title: Activepieces
item.description: Activepieces is an alternative to Zapier built with openness in mind. Users build automations called flows by chaining a trigger, such as a new form entry, to actions across apps like Google Sheets, Slack, Gmail, and CRMs. The editor is friendly to non-developers, and code steps are available for custom logic. The integrations, called pieces, are open-source and community-contributed, and each can also work as a tool for AI agents.

item.title: Komos
item.description:
Komos aims to replace fragile recorded scripts with instructions in natural language. A user describes a task, such as downloading reports from a portal or entering data across systems, and an AI agent carries it out by operating a browser, adjusting when a page changes.

That approach targets a known weakness of traditional robotic process automation, where small interface changes break bots. Enterprise teams use such tools for back-office tasks in systems that lack APIs.

item.title: leania.ai
item.description:
Leania.ai analyzes how work flows through an organization. It ingests information such as organization charts, process documentation, and meeting data, and uses AI to identify where handoffs are slow, roles overlap, or responsibilities are unclear. It then suggests changes to improve efficiency.

The audience is operations and HR leaders planning restructuring or process improvement. Outputs aim to replace guesswork with data from the company’s own materials, though recommendations still require leaders to understand context and consult the people involved.

item.title: Pipedream
item.description: Pipedream sits between no-code automation and writing everything yourself. You build workflows from triggers, such as a webhook or a new row in a sheet, and steps that either call a prebuilt action for an app or run your own code, with access to npm and PyPI packages. That mix lets developers move faster than in tools like Zapier while still handling logic that needs real programming, and it suits integrations and internal automations.
